consensus_summary: Sin is moral opposition to God, centrally expressed as rebellion, disobedience, or transgression of God’s law, while also encompassing wrongful acts, fallen condition, alienation, and an enslaving power.
book_summary: Sin is specifically the transgression of divine law; law identifies sin, and without law there is no transgression. Its opposite is righteousness.
consensus_core_identification: Moral rebellion against or violation of God’s will and standard.
boundary_disagreement: The book restricts sin to legally defined transgression, whereas the consensus also applies the term to broader rebellion, corrupt disposition, inherited fallen condition, alienation, and personified enslaving power. Those broader uses are excluded or must be reclassified as causes, conditions, or consequences rather than sin itself.
material_contradiction: There is no contradiction at the central referent: transgression of divine law is a dominant consensus meaning. The material difference is the book’s apparent exclusivity and narrower boundary.
rationale: The book preserves one of the consensus’s clearest and most widely accepted core identifications but elevates it into an exhaustive definition. Because the consensus explicitly includes law-transgression while recognizing additional biblical uses, this is a narrowing of extension rather than replacement of the referent.
strongest_objection: The cited texts strongly establish a relationship between sin and law, especially 1 John 3:4 in the KJV, but they do not by themselves prove that every biblical use of sin is exhausted by discrete legal transgression; Pauline passages can also portray sin as a ruling power or condition.
